q: Electricity is a form of energy.
e: Electricity is fundamentally a form of energy that can be transformed into other forms such as heat, mechanical, light, and sound energy.

q: There are two types of electricity: electrostatics and electrodynamics.
e: The two types of electricity are electrostatics (static electricity) and electrodynamics (current electricity).

q: Electrostatics is the study of moving electric charges and their interaction with magnetic and electric fields.
e: Electrostatics is the study of electric charge at rest. Electrodynamics is the study of moving electric charges.

q: Electric charge is the physical property of matter that causes an electric force when placed in an electromagnetic field.
e: This is the exact definition of electric charge as a physical property of matter.

q: Electric charges may be either at rest (static charges) or in motion (moving charges).
e: Electric charges can exist in a state of rest, known as static charges, or in motion, known as moving charges.

q: Flow of charges is called an electric field.
e: The flow of charges is called an electric current, not an electric field.

q: A French scientist, Du Fay, studied the nature of electric charges possessed by substances and found that there were only two kinds of charges.
e: Du Fay discovered that there are only two kinds of electric charges possessed by substances.

q: Benjamin Franklin named the two kinds of charges positive charge and negative charge.
e: Benjamin Franklin is credited with naming the two kinds of charges positive and negative.

q: Positive charge is represented by a minus sign (-).
e: Positive charge is represented by a plus sign (+), while negative charge is represented by a minus sign (-).

q: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
e: This is a fundamental principle of electrostatics: like charges repel each other, and unlike charges attract each other.

q: The closer the charges are, the greater the force between them.
e: The electric force between two charged objects increases as the distance between them decreases.

q: When two charged objects are brought together, they produce either attractive or repulsive force.
e: Depending on whether the charges are like or unlike, the resulting force will be either repulsive or attractive.

q: The electric force between two charged objects is one of the fundamental forces of nature.
e: The electric force is recognized as one of the fundamental forces of nature.

q: The electric force holds the particles that make up a molecule together.
e: The electric force holds the particles that make up an atom together, not specifically a molecule.

q: Charged objects can exert forces to other charged objects without being in contact with them.
e: Charged objects can exert forces on each other at a distance without physical contact.

q: This is possible because there is a magnetic field around each charge.
e: This is possible because there is an electric field around each charge, not a magnetic field.

q: In SI units, electric charge is measured in coulomb (C).
e: The SI unit for measuring electric charge is the coulomb (C).

q: The unit coulomb is in honour of Charles Augustin de Coulomb, a French physicist.
e: The coulomb is named after the French physicist Charles Augustin de Coulomb.

q: Coulomb discovered that the force between two charged objects depends on the magnitude of their charges and on how far apart they are.
e: Coulomb's discovery established that electric force depends on both charge magnitude and distance.

q: The magnitude of charge of an electron is $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C.
e: The fundamental charge of a single electron is exactly $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C.

q: One coulomb of charge is equivalent to the charge of $6.25 \times 10^{18}$ electrons.
e: Since one electron has a charge of $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C, one coulomb equals the charge of $6.25 \times 10^{18}$ electrons.

q: One coulomb is a relatively small value of charge.
e: One coulomb is a relatively large value of charge in the context of electrostatics.

q: 1 microcoulomb ($1 \mu$C) is equal to $10^{-6}$ C.
e: One microcoulomb is one millionth of a coulomb, which is $10^{-6}$ C.

q: Charge is one of the quantized physical quantities.
e: Electric charge is quantized, meaning it exists only in discrete, indivisible units.

q: Charge can take any arbitrary values.
e: Charge cannot take any arbitrary values; it can only take discrete values that are integral multiples of the fundamental charge.

q: Charge can only take discrete values that are integral multiples of the fundamental charge.
e: This is the definition of charge quantization, where the fundamental charge is the charge of an electron.

q: The formula for quantized charge is $Q = ne$, where $n$ is an integer.
e: In the equation $Q = ne$, $Q$ is the electric charge, $n$ is an integer, and $e$ is the charge of an electron.
